data.name: Tell Me Why
data.detailed_description:
Tell Me Why is the latest narrative adventure game from DONTNOD Entertainment, the studio behind the beloved franchise, Life is Strange. In this intimate mystery, reunited twins Tyler and Alyson Ronan use their supernatural bond to unravel the memories of their loving but troubled childhood. Set in beautiful small-town Alaska, Tell Me Why features true-to-life characters, mature themes and gripping choices.

As you conjure up memories of the past, your choices will affect the twins’ relationship, determine the strength of their bond, and shape the course of their lives.

Revisit your past, discover the truth, and shape your future

• Uncover the truth – Use the twins’ supernatural bond to relive and explore their conflicting childhood memories.

• Shape your Story – Influence the relationship between Tyler and Alyson with choices that will determine their future.

• Unlock even more secrets – Match wits with puzzles that deepen the story and open a window into the twins’ fantasy world, “The Book of Goblins.”

Experience true-to-life setting and characters

• Unique characters – Build relationships and solve mysteries through the eyes of compelling and realistic characters.

• Alaskan splendor – Explore locations set in beautiful, highly detailed small-town Alaska in stunning 4K and HDR.

Storytelling with purpose – DONTNOD Entertainment and Xbox Game Studios conducted on-the-ground research and partnered closely with cultural, mental health and gender advocates to craft a thoughtful, true-to-life experience.

reviews.review:
[h2]Overall: 6/10[/h2]

[h3]Story:[/h3]

I like the general atmosphere of the story. The vibe is easy to get on board with, it can get pretty emotional at times, and I respect how Tyler as a character has nuance and that his entire personality isn't just that "Tyler is trans." However, I'd be lying if I said I was a fan of the overall narrative itself. The reason I say this is because the writing can feel a little heavy handed/overly earnest, and the intended thematic argument is way more coherent than the way the gameplay's choice system actually expresses that same argument.
First off, in regards to the writing, it feels like this game doesn't trust its own characters, situations, or themes to communicate their meaning without explicitly explaining them. The underlying ideas are actually fairly interesting, but the dialogue repeatedly feels like it's telling you what you're supposed to take away from them. The best way I can explain it without spoiling anything is that the writing frequently follows this pattern of presenting an emotional conflict but then has the characters explain that conflict and its thematic significance to them and their struggles, as if they don't trust you to make your own conclusions. Furthermore, some of the dialogue feels less like conversations people would naturally have and more like a vehicle for communicating the writers’ thesis or something. Throughout the entire experience, these supposed trauma-ridden characters articulate their thoughts/emotions with an almost unnatural degree of clarity, explicitly discussing memory, subjective experience, and why their differing perspectives have created a rift between them. It just makes them feel less like people discovering/struggling with these ideas and more like a storyboard explaining the narrative to the player. Instead of allowing you to interpret the twins as individuals, the story often has them explain what an event means to them and why it affected them, so the emotional meaning is [i]delivered[/i] rather than [i]discovered.[/i] Like, a subtler approach might have Tyler become uneasy, avoid a subject, or react in a way that suggests what he's feeling during dialogue about uncomfortable topics, which would allow you to infer the meaning. I genuinely think the themes themselves are interesting, but the problem is that the writing spells them out so explicitly that the execution falls pretty flat.
Next, my second biggest issue is that despite the initial framing, the story isn't really about [spoiler]discovering the objective truth of Mary-Ann's death.[/spoiler] It's about how Tyler and Alyson have constructed different versions of their childhood, how those versions have become part of their identities, and whether they can accept that they have grown into different people. However, from the first episode, the narrative packages that idea inside a mystery-style plot structure that strongly encourages you to think, "Okay, but which one of them is actually remembering this correctly?" and that's where the writing REALLY starts fighting itself, in my opinion.
You're repeatedly presented with situations where the twins remember important events very differently, and you're then asked to choose which memory you believe, but I think that's a strange thing to ask the player to do when the entire premise is that memory is subjective and affected by trauma. The story seems to want you to understand that "well, neither twin's recollection is necessarily an [i]objective[/i] recording of what happened due to how people's varied perceptions can interpret events!" but then the relationship system consistently says: Tyler's memory = strengthened bond, Alyson's memory = weakened bond. It becomes awkward after a while because you're occasionally given contextual information suggesting that one twin's interpretation is more credible than the other's, yet the plot often puts things in a bizarre position where the intellectually honest response can be: "I don't think Tyler remembers this correctly (or vice versa)" but the story treats this as the twin's relationship being damaged. That's not really a moral choice; it's a relationship-meter choice disguised as a philosophical choice.
Not only does it largely disregard the whole "mystery vibe" established very early on, but it also feels like you're being forced either to invalidate one character's feelings (even when they're obviously misremembering) in order to get to the truth, or choose to side with the opposing twin's viewpoint for the sake of maintaining their "bond" rather than actually discovering what happened, and that's a pretty fundamental design problem given what the story is apparently trying to accomplish.

[h3]Gameplay:[/h3]

The gameplay takes a pretty significant backseat to the narrative, which isn't necessarily a problem for a game this heavily focused on its story, but I did feel like there were extended stretches where there was very little to actually interact with. Most of the gameplay consists of walking around, examining objects, talking to characters, triggering memories, and occasionally solving a simple puzzle, with the exploration and puzzles mostly serving as ways to facilitate the story rather than being particularly clever or engaging on their own. I didn't outright hate the gameplay, but there were definitely times when it felt like I was barely playing anything at all. Even for a narrative-driven game, this one right here can go surprisingly long without giving you much meaningful interactivity, making some sections feel more like watching the mediocre story unfold than actually participating in it.

[h3]World:[/h3]

I really like the general atmosphere and location. Alaska is an interesting setting, especially because games don't often take place in such environments, and I appreciate that it isn't just another generic city or suburb. The environments themselves are also generally believable and do a good job of making each scene/level feel like an actual small town. However, the problem is that the longer you spend in each location, the more hollow they start to feel. They're mostly linear spaces built to forward convos/story beats rather than places that feel genuinely explorable or informational to general context about Delos Crossing outside of what the story requires you to know. It's a shame because the vibes from each building give this game a strong sense of place, but the level design doesn't really take advantage of it beyond making convincing-looking backdrops for the narrative.

[h3]Visuals:[/h3]

I honestly didn't have much of an issue with the graphics. The stylized art direction works well for a AA game and it's a large part of what makes up the atmosphere due to the somber color palette, snowy environments, and soft lighting that gives everything a melancholic tone. The character models and animations aren't always the most technically impressive, but I think the overall presentation holds up well enough for what the game is trying to be. More importantly though, the game ran extremely well for me, with no noticeable performance issues, bugs, or other technical problems getting in the way.

[h3]Music/Sound Design:[/h3]

The music and sound design are easily some of the strongest aspects. I really like the OST's overall sound, especially the way its subtle, atmospheric quality fits the melancholic and introspective moments without becoming too distracting or overly dramatic. The environmental sound design works well alongside it too, but it's significantly less noteworthy, in my opinion. None of it is particularly flashy, but I think the combination of the music, ambient sound, and overall audio presentation gives everything a really distinct and enjoyable energy. My biggest criticism is that the voice acting can be a little stiff or cringe at times, but that's more of a weakness with the performances than the audio direction itself, and it was never too much of a problem anyway.
